html:
Around 779 King Trisong Detsen of the Tibetan Empire made Buddhism the state religion of Tibet, after the consecration of Samye, the first Buddhist monastery in the country.

Buddhism had reached the Tibetan court more than a century earlier, under Songtsen Gampo, but it had powerful enemies among nobles who backed the older rites of the Bon tradition and the native priests. Trisong Detsen, who reigned from 755 to 797, came down firmly on the Buddhist side.

He invited teachers from India:

  • Shantarakshita, a scholar abbot from the great monastery of Nalanda
  • Padmasambhava, a tantric master who in Tibetan memory tamed the local spirits that resisted the new faith

With them he founded the Samye Monastery, where the first Tibetans were ordained as monks. A royal edict, carved on a pillar at Samye, bound the king and his heirs to support Buddhism. Teams began translating Sanskrit texts into Tibetan.

Tibet then had to choose between Indian and Chinese forms of Buddhism. Tradition says a great debate was held at Samye in the 790s, and the Indian side won. Tibetan Buddhism has followed Indian models ever since.

Trisong Detsen is remembered as the second of the three Dharma Kings. The empire fell in 842, but the Buddhism he planted grew into the faith of Tibet and Mongolia.
sum: Around 779 King Trisong Detsen of the Tibetan Empire made Buddhism the state religion of Tibet, after the consecration of Samye, the first Buddhist monastery in the country.
